prompt: What reaction do aldolase enzymes catalyze?

choices.text: The addition of a ketone enolate ion to an aldehyde
The addition of an ester enolate ion to a thioester
choices.why: That describes a Claisen condensation, such as those in fatty-acid biosynthesis.

choices.text: The dehydration of a β-hydroxy ketone to an enone
choices.why: Aldolases catalyze the aldol addition itself, joining two partners.

choices.text: The hydrolysis of an ester to a carboxylic acid
choices.why: Aldolases join a ketone enolate ion to an aldehyde; no ester is hydrolyzed.

explanation: Aldolases, common in carbohydrate metabolism, catalyze the addition of a ketone enolate ion to an aldehyde.

prompt: How do type I aldolases, found primarily in animals and higher plants, operate?

choices.text: Through an enamine
Through an enolate ion formed with the help of a Zn^2+ ion
choices.why: That is how type II aldolases, found primarily in fungi and bacteria, work.

choices.text: Through a metal-bound carbocation
choices.why: Type I aldolases use an enamine; it is type II that uses a metal ion, as a Lewis acid.

choices.text: By a Claisen condensation with a thioester
choices.why: Aldolases catalyze aldol reactions, not Claisen condensations.

explanation: Both types of aldolase catalyze the same kind of reaction, but type I aldolases operate through an enamine, while type II aldolases require a metal ion (usually Zn^2+) as a Lewis acid and operate through an enolate ion.

prompt: Which statement describes type II aldolases?

choices.text: Found mainly in fungi and bacteria; they use a metal ion (usually Zn^2+) and an enolate ion
Found mainly in animals and higher plants; they operate through an enamine
choices.why: That describes type I aldolases.

choices.text: Found mainly in fungi and bacteria; they use an enamine formed with a lysine
choices.why: The lysine enamine route belongs to type I aldolases, in animals and higher plants.

choices.text: Found only in animals; they need no metal ion and use an enolate ion
choices.why: Type II aldolases occur primarily in fungi and bacteria, and they require a metal ion.

explanation: Type I aldolases occur primarily in animals and higher plants and operate through an enamine. Type II aldolases occur primarily in fungi and bacteria; they require a metal ion, usually Zn^2+, as a Lewis acid and operate through an enolate ion.

prompt: In glucose biosynthesis, what does the aldolase-catalyzed reaction of dihydroxyacetone phosphate with glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate give?

choices.text: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate
Acetoacetyl ACP
choices.why: Acetoacetyl ACP is a product of a Claisen condensation in fatty-acid biosynthesis.

choices.text: 3-Ketohexanoyl ACP
choices.why: That comes from the mixed Claisen condensation of butyryl synthase with malonyl ACP.

choices.text: Two molecules of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate
choices.why: The aldolase joins the two three-carbon partners into one product.

explanation: An example of an aldolase-catalyzed reaction occurs in glucose biosynthesis, when dihydroxyacetone phosphate reacts with glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate to give fructose 1,6-bisphosphate.

prompt: In animals and higher plants, dihydroxyacetone phosphate is converted into an enamine by reaction with which group on the aldolase?

choices.text: The –NH2 group of a lysine
The –SH group of a synthase
choices.why: The synthase –SH group appears in fatty-acid biosynthesis, where it forms thioesters.

choices.text: A bound Zn^2+ ion
choices.why: Zn^2+ is used by type II aldolases in bacteria and fungi, which operate through an enolate ion, not an enamine.

choices.text: An acyl carrier protein
choices.why: Acyl carrier protein (ACP) forms thioester bonds to acyl groups in fatty-acid biosynthesis.

explanation: In animals and higher plants, dihydroxyacetone phosphate is first converted into an enamine by reaction with the –NH2 group on a lysine in the enzyme. The enamine adds to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, and the iminium ion that results is hydrolyzed.

prompt: Mixed aldol reactions often give mixtures in the laboratory. Why are aldolase-catalyzed mixed aldol reactions successful in living systems?

choices.text: Because of the selectivity of the enzyme catalysts
Because one partner always has no α hydrogens
choices.why: That is a laboratory strategy; the section credits the enzymes' selectivity.

choices.text: Because the two partners are always identical
choices.why: Aldolase reactions are mixed aldol reactions, between two different partners.

choices.text: Because biological aldol reactions are irreversible
choices.why: The section's explanation is enzyme selectivity, not irreversibility.

explanation: Aldolase-catalyzed reactions are mixed aldol reactions between two different partners. Such reactions often give mixtures in the laboratory but are successful in living systems because of the selectivity of the enzyme catalysts.

prompt: In fatty-acid biosynthesis, how is the enolate ion that carries out the Claisen condensation generated?

choices.text: By decarboxylation of malonyl ACP
By removing an α hydrogen with sodium ethoxide
choices.why: That is how ester enolates are made in the laboratory. In the cell the enolate comes from decarboxylation.

choices.text: By forming an enamine with a lysine in the enzyme
choices.why: That is how type I aldolases work in aldol reactions.

choices.text: By complexing a carbonyl group with Zn^2+
choices.why: Zn^2+ is used by type II aldolases, not in this Claisen condensation.

explanation: An enolate ion generated by decarboxylation of malonyl ACP adds to the carbonyl group of an acyl group bonded through a thioester linkage to a synthase enzyme. The tetrahedral intermediate expels the synthase, giving acetoacetyl ACP. ACP stands for acyl carrier protein.

prompt: What does butyryl synthase give in its mixed Claisen condensation with malonyl ACP?

choices.text: 3-Ketohexanoyl ACP
Acetoacetyl ACP
choices.why: Acetoacetyl ACP comes from an acetyl group on the synthase. A butyryl group gives a longer chain.

choices.text: 3-Ketoheptanoyl ACP
choices.why: The malonyl group loses CO2 when its enolate forms, so it adds only two carbons to the four-carbon butyryl group.

choices.text: 3-Hydroxyhexanoyl ACP
choices.why: In a Claisen condensation the tetrahedral intermediate expels the synthase, leaving a ketone, not an alcohol.

explanation: Butyryl synthase reacts with malonyl ACP in a mixed Claisen condensation to give 3-ketohexanoyl ACP, a six-carbon chain with carbonyl groups on carbons 1 and 3.

prompt: In fatty-acid biosynthesis, an acetyl group (two carbons) on the synthase reacts with malonyl ACP, whose malonyl group has three carbons and loses CO2. How many carbons are in the acyl chain of the acetoacetyl ACP product?
explanation: Decarboxylation of malonyl ACP removes one carbon as CO2, leaving a two-carbon enolate. It adds to the two-carbon acetyl group, giving the four-carbon acetoacetyl group: 2 + 3 − 1 = 4.

prompt: Dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate each have a three-carbon chain. How many carbons are in the chain of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, their aldol product?
explanation: An aldol reaction joins the two partners without losing any carbons, so fructose 1,6-bisphosphate has 3 + 3 = 6 carbons in its chain.
